meta.description: Not Agatha Christie. The line first appeared 2 April 1969 under the ‘Senator Soaper’ name, and belongs to columnist Bill Vaughan.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'To Err is Human; To Really Foul Things Up Requires a Computer'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Agatha Christie. Quote Investigator traces it to a 2 April 1969 ‘Senator Soaper’ paragraph by Kansas City Star columnist Bill Vaughan.

answer.label: Not Agatha Christie — actually Bill Vaughan
answer.authorDates: 1915–1977 · Kansas City Star columnist, who wrote the syndicated Senator Soaper column
answer.sourceLine: The earliest printing Quote Investigator has found is 2 April 1969, in the Free Lance-Star of Fredericksburg, Virginia ↗, as a free-standing paragraph under the name ‘Senator Soaper’ — the comic alter ego of Kansas City Star columnist Bill Vaughan, who carried the line under his own byline four days later. Agatha Christie’s name is attached because Hallowe’en Party, published later the same year, contains a different computer joke built on the same Pope proverb; the wording above is not hers.

source.excerpt: To err is human; to really foul things up requires a computer.
trail: 2 April 1969 — the earliest close match located by Quote Investigator ↗, printed in the Free Lance-Star under the name of the imaginary legislator ‘Senator Soaper’. Bill Vaughan had written that syndicated feature since taking it over from Harry V. Wade in 1953.

6 April 1969 — the same line leads the “Senator Soaper Says:” column with Vaughan’s byline in the Independent Press-Telegram; by 1970 Dorothy Sarnoff prints it in Speech Can Change Your Life with the credit ‘BILL VAUGHAN’ attached, both per QI ↗.

November 1969 — Agatha Christie’s Hallowe’en Party is published by the Collins Crime Club, with a US edition from Dodd, Mead the same year ↗. It contains a different computer joke, spoken by Ariadne Oliver — QI credits Christie with that sentence, and notes that because book composition timelines are unknown, which writer got there first cannot be settled.

1982 onward — Paul Ehrlich picks up the credit in A Dictionary of Contemporary Quotations and later in newspaper filler, while the Oxford, Yale and Columbia quotation dictionaries all carry the line as anonymous — QI finds no early support for Ehrlich ↗.
source.excerptNote: It ran as a free-standing paragraph on page one under the standing name ‘Senator Soaper’ — no article, no set-up, no byline. Four days later the same line led the “Senator Soaper Says:” column with Vaughan’s name on it, and the day after that the Hartford Courant ran it with no attribution at all.

source.rightsNote: The wording is a 1969 American newspaper column item, so it falls well after the pre-1931 line for US public domain and should be treated as in copyright. The same is true of the Christie passage often confused with it: Hallowe’en Party was first published in 1969 (Collins Crime Club, UK; Dodd, Mead, US) and remains under the control of the Christie estate and its publishers. Short attributed quotation for commentary and criticism is a separate question from reproduction.

author.name: Bill Vaughan
author.heading: The paragrapher behind ‘Senator Soaper’
author.bio: William Edward ‘Bill’ Vaughan (8 October 1915 – 25 February 1977) was born in St. Louis and wrote a syndicated column for the Kansas City Star from 1946 until his death. He was a paragrapher — a specialist in the one- or two-sentence newspaper joke — and took over the long-running syndicated feature ‘Senator Soaper Says’ from Harry V. Wade in 1953, voicing it through an imaginary legislator. Time profiled him in 1962 as a ‘Star Paragrapher’, and noted that his lines were widely reprinted without credit, which is exactly what happened to this one.

misattribution.heading: Who it gets pinned on, and why
misattribution.intro: This line has attracted three separate false owners: a novelist who wrote a different joke the same year, a biologist credited a decade later with no evidence, and ‘Anonymous’ — the default whenever a newspaper paragraph outlives its byline.

items.why: Christie wrote a computer joke, but not this one. In Hallowe’en Party (1969) Mrs Oliver tells Poirot: “I know there’s a proverb which says, ‘To err is human’ but a human error is nothing to what a computer can do if it tries.” Quote Investigator credits Christie with that sentence ↗ — and Bill Vaughan with the ‘foul things up’ wording. The two get merged, and Christie’s is the famous name, so hers is the one that sticks.

Quote Investigator ↗ reports that Jonathon Green’s A Dictionary of Contemporary Quotations (1982) credited the biologist Paul Ehrlich, sourcing it to the Farmers Almanac of 1978, and that newspapers repeated the Ehrlich credit in 1992. QI has located no comparably early citation supporting him.
The Oxford Dictionary of Quotations, the Yale Book of Quotations and the Columbia Dictionary of Quotations all print the adage without an author, according to QI’s survey of the three ↗.
“To err is human” really is Pope’s, from An Essay on Criticism ↗ — but the computer half is a twentieth-century joke bolted onto it, and Pope is sometimes cited as though he owned the whole sentence.

misattribution.truthLine: On the evidence assembled by Quote Investigator ↗, the earliest known printing is 2 April 1969 under the ‘Senator Soaper’ name, with Bill Vaughan’s byline on it four days later — and QI’s own verdict is that Vaughan “should receive credit for now.”

context.heading: Two computer jokes, one 1711 proverb, the same year
lead: Bill Vaughan wrote for a vanished newspaper genre: the paragraph, a self-contained joke of one or two lines dropped into a column with no set-up and no punchline beyond itself. That format is precisely why this line lost its author. As Vaughan himself told Time in 1962, in a profile quoted by Quote Investigator ↗, paragraphing was a trade of borrowed lines — funny, portable, and easy to reprint without a name attached.

The coincidence that muddied the water is real: in the same year, Agatha Christie published Hallowe’en Party, in which Mrs Oliver needles Poirot about his electric-light bill and twists the same Alexander Pope proverb toward computers. Quote Investigator credits Christie with her own line ↗ and Vaughan with this one, while noting the ordering of composition cannot be established — and even raising the possibility that Vaughan was influenced by Christie’s passage.
context.detailsSummary: The Pope line underneath both jokes
detailsBody: Both quips are variations on Alexander Pope’s An Essay on Criticism, first published in 1711 and reprinted in Pope’s 1717 collected Works ↗. Quote Investigator notes that the 1711 printing used the older spelling ‘Humane’, and that a later edition’s title page dated the poem’s composition to 1709.

Vaughan’s version spread fast and anonymously. By August 1969 a West Virginia columnist reported it as graffiti; by 1980 the Washington Post noted you could buy it on a novelty plaque. Neither carried his name.
context.pull: Paragraphing was always based on a firm foundation of mutual plagiarism.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator's earliest close match for “To err is human; to really foul things up requires a computer” is 2 April 1969 in the Free Lance-Star, credited to ‘Senator Soaper’, the alter ego of columnist Bill Vaughan; QI concludes Vaughan should receive credit. It also records the 6 April 1969 Vaughan byline in the Independent Press-Telegram, the 1970 Dorothy Sarnoff credit (p. 288), the August 1969 graffito report, the 1980 Washington Post plaque mention, the 1982 Dictionary of Contemporary Quotations credit to Paul Ehrlich sourced to the Farmers Almanac 1978, the 1992 newspaper Ehrlich attributions, and that the Oxford, Yale and Columbia quotation references all present the adage as anonymous. QI also quotes Vaughan in Time (1962) on paragraphing resting on ‘mutual plagiarism’, notes he took over Senator Soaper from Harry V. Wade in 1953, and says it is possible Vaughan was influenced by the Agatha Christie passage.

Quote Investigator quotes the Hallowe'en Party (1969) exchange in which Mrs Oliver tells Poirot “I know there’s a proverb which says, ‘To err is human’ but a human error is nothing to what a computer can do if it tries”, concludes that Agatha Christie should be credited with that statement, and states that because book composition timelines are unknown the chronology against Vaughan's April 1969 line is uncertain.

William E. ‘Bill’ Vaughan (8 October 1915 – 25 February 1977) was an American columnist and author, born in St. Louis, Missouri, who wrote a syndicated column for the Kansas City Star from 1946 until his death.

Wikiquote's Agatha Christie page lists, under Hallowe'en Party (1969) and attributed to Ariadne Oliver, the line “I know there’s a proverb which says, ‘To err is human’ but a human error is nothing to what a computer can do if it tries”; the ‘foul things up’ wording does not appear on the page.

Hallowe'en Party was first published in the United Kingdom by the Collins Crime Club in November 1969 and in the United States by Dodd, Mead and Company later the same year; it features Hercule Poirot and the novelist Ariadne Oliver.
The 1717 edition of Pope's Works contains An Essay on Criticism including the couplet on erring being human and forgiving divine.
